sections.h2: Can someone living in a Tennessee house become its owner by adverse possession?
sections.html:
Only by meeting a demanding test over a long stretch of time, and in 2024 the Tennessee Supreme Court spelled out what the adversity part of that test requires. Under the doctrine, a person can gain legal title, or a defense to the owner's lawsuit, by keeping exclusive, actual, adverse, continuous, open and notorious possession for the period the law requires.

The rules sit in Tenn. Code Ann. Title 28, chapter 2, part 1, alongside a body of common law. A 2000 bill to extend them to short-line railways described "all statutory and common law relative to adverse possession," which is a fair summary of the structure. The time periods and the exceptions are technical, so an owner facing a real claim should get the parcel's facts in front of a Tennessee attorney early.

A person who simply moves into a vacant house, or who stays after permission ends, is not automatically on the road to ownership. The next section explains why adversity is the sticking point.

sections.h2: What did the Tennessee Supreme Court decide in Mathes v. 99 Hermitage?
sections.html:
The Court held that adversity, for both common-law and statutory adverse possession, requires either a conflict of title or a controversy about the right to possess the property. Justice Sarah K. Campbell wrote the opinion, issued July 31, 2024, in a case that began in chancery court.

The facts show how a real owner can still lose a possession fight. Ora Eads, Jr. obtained legal title to a commercial property near downtown Nashville but did not register the deed. About twenty years later, the person who had sold the property to him defaulted on a loan, and the lender's judgment lien led to a sale. The plaintiffs argued he had adversely possessed the property during the gap. The Court rejected that argument because neither a title conflict nor a possession dispute existed for the required time.

  • An unregistered deed sat in the chain while the seller's creditor pursued the property.
  • Long, quiet use of land does not by itself satisfy the adversity element.
  • The opinion reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the chancery court's judgment.

The practical lesson for Tennessee owners is to record every deed promptly with the county register of deeds. The register's fee in Davidson County starts at a $10 minimum plus a $2 data processing fee, which is small next to the risk Eads carried.

sections.h2: How does a Tennessee owner remove someone who has no right to be there?
sections.html:
Through a detainer warrant in general sessions court. Tennessee law recognizes three types under Title 29, chapter 18: forcible entry and detainer (29-18-102), forcible detainer (29-18-103) and unlawful detainer (29-18-104). Which one fits depends on how the person came to be in the house, such as a tenant who stayed past the lease or an occupant who entered without permission.

A summons can be served on any adult found in possession of the premises, including an adult who simply occupies it, and service on that person is enough to let the owner regain the property. When nobody is found, the court's own training materials describe a posting route. The plaintiff first tries personal service on three different dates and writes each attempt on the face of the warrant. After the third failed attempt, the plaintiff posts a copy on the door, mails the warrant and makes a note on the warrant. The posting has to go up at least six days before the hearing.

Detainer warrant timing in Tennessee general sessions court
StepWhat the courts' landlord-tenant presentation says
Service on an occupantSummons may be served on any adult found in possession
Service by postingThree attempts on different dates, then door posting, mailing and a notation, at least six days before the hearing
ContinuanceFifteen days at most, unless the parties agree, the landlord consents or no court is being held
Writ of possessionExecuted immediately once awarded after judgment for the plaintiff
Appeal to circuit courtTen days under Tenn. Code Ann. 27-5-108
Certiorari and supersedeasThirty days, with a bond and a stated meritorious reason

Source: Tennessee Courts, Landlord Tenant Update presentation (Mike King).

sections.h2: What happens if the occupant appeals the detainer judgment?
sections.html:
The presentation lays out a bond rule that favors a plaintiff who has already won. A defendant who appeals must post a bond covering one year of rent. If the defendant does not post that bond, the plaintiff does not have to post a bond of its own to obtain possession. The plaintiff is entitled to interest on the judgment, running from the judgment date, if the appeal fails.

When the defendant does post the bond, the plaintiff must execute a bond in double the value of one year's rent, conditioned on paying costs and damages from any wrongful enforcement of the writ. A defendant who seeks circuit court review by certiorari must post a bond covering costs and damages, and when the defendant is the applicant the bond must also cover rent during the litigation.

These are procedural details an attorney handles, but they explain why a contested removal can take longer than the first hearing suggests.

sections.h2: Who actually carries out the removal?
sections.html:
The county sheriff executes the writ. The UT County Technical Assistance Service, in its electronic library for county officials, says a writ of restitution is not executed until the sheriff delivers actual possession of the premises to the plaintiff and leaves the plaintiff in quiet possession. If the occupant does not leave peacefully, removing the person is the officer's duty. Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18-127 authorizes force where needed.

  • The officer oversees the procedure and keeps the peace. Officers should not act as the plaintiff's movers.
  • The plaintiff is responsible for removing and storing the occupant's belongings.
  • Hazardous items, such as weapons or prescription medications, are to be inventoried and secured.
  • Entering the wrong residence is a recurring source of lawsuits, so the address on the writ should be checked against the parcel.

An owner should never change locks or remove an occupant's belongings on their own authority. The court process exists so that the sheriff, not the owner, performs the removal.

sections.h2: Do different rules apply when the occupant is a former tenant?
sections.html:
Yes. Tennessee has two landlord-tenant regimes. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies in Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson counties. Every other county falls under Tenn. Code Ann. 66-7-101 and following.

The presentation describes URLTA notices of fourteen, seven and three days, depending on the violation, and a five-day grace period on rent. Outside URLTA counties it lists fourteen-day, thirty-day and three-day notices. It also stresses that written notice is required and that the owner must rely in court on the reasons stated in the notice. If new misconduct occurs after the notice, a new notice is needed.

That detail matters for a seller. A buyer or a title company will ask who lives in the house and on what terms, and a clean court record of a completed detainer case answers the question better than a verbal promise to leave.

sections.h2: How does an occupied or disputed house affect a sale?
sections.html:
The owner's first job is to establish who holds title. Pull the recorded deed, confirm the owner of record in the register of deeds' office, and make sure no gap like the one in Mathes exists in your chain. If a stranger claims an interest, expect a title company to require that claim to be resolved before closing.

  • Gather the recorded deed and any loan or lien paperwork.
  • Write down when the occupant arrived and whether you ever gave permission.
  • Keep copies of notices, texts and rent records.
  • File the detainer warrant in the general sessions court of the county where the house sits.

Some buyers who purchase as-is will take an occupied property, but the occupant's situation will shape the price and the timeline. Describe the facts plainly when you ask for an offer.

faqs.q: Can a squatter take my Tennessee house?
faqs.a: Only through adverse possession, which requires exclusive, actual, adverse, continuous, open and notorious possession for the period the law sets. The Tennessee Supreme Court held in 2024 that adversity requires a conflict of title or a controversy over the right to possess.

faqs.q: How do I remove an occupant who is not a tenant?
faqs.a: File a detainer warrant in general sessions court. Tennessee recognizes forcible entry and detainer, forcible detainer and unlawful detainer under Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18-102 through 29-18-104.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks myself?
faqs.a: No. Removal is carried out by the sheriff under a writ, and the CTAS guidance says the writ is not executed until the sheriff delivers actual possession to the plaintiff.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a general sessions detainer ruling?
faqs.a: Ten days under Tenn. Code Ann. 27-5-108. A separate route, certiorari and supersedeas to circuit court, must be sought within thirty days and requires a bond.

faqs.q: What if I cannot find the person to serve?
faqs.a: After three documented attempts on different dates, the plaintiff may post the warrant on the door, mail it and note the steps on the warrant, at least six days before the hearing. Posting supports possession but not a money judgment.
